title: Bleached corals thrive within days when touching healthy neighbour (nature.com)
comments: Coral gets its color from algae called zooxanthellae, which it depends on for photosynthesis.Bleaching is actually due to the coral expelling those algae. Bleached corals are not dead, and remarkably they can not only let the algae in again but can also select a different algae species to cultivate (changing colour in the process)!.This is thought to be a deliberate survival strategy to optimize the species of algae under different conditions (Adaptive Bleaching Hypothesis).Bleaching is caused by the same stressors (like high temperature) which kill coral, but bleaching itself is not death of the coral.reply
> Bleaching is actually due to the coral expelling those algaeDue to the coral or due to the algae? Put another way, could we engineer UV resistance into the algae?reply
It's not UV that's the problem but heat. We could possibly cultivate algae that are more heat resistant?reply

I'm not an expert, but yes we can and we do.And so does the coral!If a species of algae cannot handle high temperatures without generating chemicals like hydrogen peroxide which trigger the bleaching, then that species is ejected sooner and more frequently during warmer months, creating selective pressure for species that can.To survive these conditions without getting ejected, the algae need to essentially run their photosynthesis process more slowly. They produce less chlorophyll per cell and create sacrificial 'photoprotective carotenoid pigments' which act like sunscreen and dissipate that potential sunlight energy as useless heat (coral has a few tricks too fluorescent proteins).So the coral is actually in a delicate balancing act, selecting the most aggressive/productive algae which won't also try to kill it during summer. Corals will learn to be more conservative in their selection and algae will get more conservative themselves. We want this process to happen quickly enough so that we don't lose coral coverage and diversity in the coming decades / centuries, but we can be confident that on longer timescales the coral will adapt, assuming we don't get runaway warming.reply
This is actually in process, though my understanding is that it doesn't seem to keep up with the pace of ocean temperature rise.https://www.npr.org/2024/04/17/1245085914/coral-reefs-bleach...reply

Having been a diver on the Great Barrier Reef numerous times, the scale of bleaching events means that there is often no non-bleached neighbour for vast distances. Healthy propagation rarely occurs before the brown sludge sets in, then its game over.reply

This kills me. I saw the reef for the first time around 2007. I went back twice, and the last time I was there (2017) I honestly couldn't believe what I saw. Wasteland? An under water desert? I don't have words for it, but I don't really want to go back because it hit me so hard. Our planet is dying and we're sitting here debating why/who and not doing anywhere near enough to fix it.I'm so glad we have space rockets, flying cars and drone warfare...but I'd trade it all in for the reef to come back.reply

> I'm so glad we have space rockets, flying cars and drone warfare...but I'd trade it all in for the reef to come back.It's really just climate change. (Ocean warming is what causes bleaching.) Luckily, since the 80s we've had the technology to generate energy without releasing greenhouse gases. I wish more people knew about the harms caused by climate change because maybe if they were they'd be more interested in preventing them.reply

I feel like the harms were really drilled into Millennials like myself but then we seem to have assumed that younger Gen Zs and gen Alpha will just receive the climate change wisdom via osmosis or maybe if we're lucky, their parents. I've seen more people worrying about under-population (under population! Remember over-population?) than the environment recently. Maybe we need to bring Captain Planet back.reply

To be fair, overpopulation was never an actual concern. Since the 1800s, food production growth rates have outpaced population growth rates. Underpopulation _is_ a concern when infrastructure and social structures may not be able contract quickly enough to sustain our current quality of life.reply

title: Dam removals are bringing fish back across the northeastern United States (smithsonianmag.com)
comments: A rewilding organization bought some forest land, downstream from a dam, that used to get seasonal flooding before the dam was built and made an agreement with the dam operators to do artificial seasonal flooding via ditches they dug. The flooded forest has the effect of providing fish nurseries so hatchlings have a chance to hide and grow before the water recedes and they have to return to the river.https://youtu.be/qcVMX32c0ioI think it's a testament that human activity and nature don't have to be all or nothing, but we need to consider and mitigate the impact of our actions and always leave space for nature.reply
Exactly I don't get why we can't figure out and prioritize allowing fish to pass around the dams.reply
We can.  One presumes it is less efficient than just removing the dam.  It is more work versus less work - fish ladders and the like.reply
Not only that, but a lot of these dams are not even in use any more, so doing additional work doesn't make much sense. Remove the dam, remove the problem, instead of duct tape solutions.reply

Fisherman like them because fish bunch up beneath them.  Despite the overall populations being higher once all the dams are gone.There is an aspect of property value as well - dams maintain a certain river level and removal may impact how nice people's river houses are.  (Source:  Dam near me partly removed, turned into a kayak course.)reply
There are many dams with fish ladders or even fish cannons.reply

title: Furifont, a Japanese font that shows furigana (antfu.me)
comments: I think this is a rare “useful” abuse of font ligatures, and in that respect I think this is a cool project, but it's also a terrible idea that nobody should actually use, because Japanese kanji readings are famously ambiguous and context-dependent. The modal character has two different readings without counting those used in personal names, nor contextual slight changes to pronunciation. Some characters have six different readings, and that's again without counting those used in personal names. There's no way a font can do a good job at it unless you can somehow stuff an entire LLM in there.For context, it's a hard enough problem that Google Translate's own romanised pronunciation guides are frequently wrong, or disagree with their text-to-speech.reply

I agree, and if anything the problem is even worse. You mentioned characters with 6 readings, here's one with more than 30:https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E7%94%9FAnd while you can usually figure out which reading applies based on what follows, there are still many cases where you can't. A standalone 今日 can be any of "konnichi", "kyou" or "konjitsu" depending on context and intent.reply
> unless you can somehow stuff an entire LLM in there.Well, it wouldn't be the first time ;)https://fuglede.github.io/llama.ttf/reply
Was thinking of exactly this one as well.reply

Yeah. I also notice that Google Translate's guess at pronunciation frequently has errors, and that IS a LLM.Someone further downthread said it appears to have about 80% accuracy on a short sentence, which means if you're not already at a level of skill where you can verify, then it's going to teach you the wrong pronunciations constantly. When studying languages myself, I find that learning the wrong pronunciation for something is annoyingly sticky, and unlearning takes more effort than learning something correctly the first time.reply
> There's no way a font can do a good job at it unless you can somehow stuff an entire LLM in there.I’d say you can do a pretty good job with conditional random fields.reply

Pretty good job, meaning that you get 96% there (if I recall correctly the results for MeCab which uses CRF). But 4% of kanji words is still multiple wrong furigana per page.Still, very cool demo!reply

Yeah, I already see a few mistakes just looking at this page.
But I guess still useful?reply

Yeah. I experimented with a random Japanese news article. Scanning it with my eyeballs, I found:    Correct .. 80 chars
    Missing .. 12 chars
    Wrong ....  8 chars

So I guess the accuracy is roughly 80%. Maybe useful, but not super reliable.reply

Don't use it as the main font in a japanese textbook, sure, but use it with the disclaimer that it's not perfect and will get some readings wrong? Why not, still pretty useful. title: The Commodore 64 hardware simulator: break chips and pins, see the results (github.com/antirez)
comments: This is really cool, and a fantastic piece of work. It may come in handy when diagnosing / fixing C64 boards.Stretch goals:* Allow the simulation to run diagnostics carts.* On the 250407 board I have had timing edge cases with PLA replacements - the fix is often to fit a small (~100pF) capacitor on the /CASRAM line to slow it down a bit. The cap is fitted from the left leg of an existing 82 Ohm resistor and a nearby ground point close to 'RAM6'. Some boards actually have official space for the capacitor - designated C204. With some original PLA variants on real boards the capacitor may already be fitted. It would be good to be able to enable and disable this capacitor and set its value to see the effects.Write-up: https://linker3000.com/index.php/blog/poor64reply

I remember Byuu (RIP) wrote an article around ~10 years ago talking about why BSNES/Higan was "slow", explaining that it's really not slow given what it's trying to do.  The more accurately you simulate the chips, there is simply more over overhead involved with synchronization and whatnot.I remember in that article they mentioned a Pong circuit simulation like this that was getting something along the lines of 10FPS of gameplay, which astonished me.  You don't get a lot simpler of a game than Pong and even on amazing hardware it was still unplayable if you want the truest form of emulation.reply

They use tartrazine that is a common dye for food, not crushed Doritos. They need a lot of dye to change the internal refraction index and make the meat transparent. So they choose it. From the research article https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11931656/> It is a hygroscopic compound with a high solubility in water and minimal reactivity. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) has concluded that this molecule exhibits no adverse effects or systemic toxicity at doses up to 2 g per kilogram of body weight (14). Vertebrate blood is one thing that is opaque due to hemoglobin, and it cannot be made transparent. The same is true for the pigmented retina of the eyes. So transparent frogs and fishes still have opaque eyes and blood vessels.Where pigments like the heme of the blood or the melanin of the skin or the visual pigments of the retina are absent, the opacity is due only to the variable refractive index, which causes light scattering, and in this case the tissue can be made transparent with methods like that described in the article which make the refractive index uniform (i.e. exactly like snow that transitions from opaque to transparent when melting).reply

title: NY announces game ownership bill requiring ownership rather than licensing (tomshardware.com)
comments: Fully in support of this, but it will never happen, at least not for digital purchases, for a simple economic reason: the internet enables far too efficient a market and it'd wreck businesses with the first sale doctrine. One game sold by the publisher would then be constantly resold by endusers with an ever decreasing price to the point that you could probably buy most of any game for a couple of bucks a year or so after release. The reason this doesn't already happen with physical copies is because there's tedium + cost involved in the transfer, and they also create a motivation to collect. It's somehow enjoyable see a shelf full of games, music, movies, or whatever else.More realistic would be improving copyright law. I think it'd be reasonable to state that copyright lasts 20 years from the first 'transfer' (sell, licensing, etc) of a creation. 20 years is long enough to fully monetize, but also short enough to really enable some interesting acceleration/derivation in society. For instance just about now XBox 360 games would be coming out of copyright protection. That seems perfectly reasonable, especially in the era of LLMs where 'sidestepping' copyright is going to be increasingly trivial anyhow.reply

I suppose they'll just have to give up on selling games in the US.Do you think it's possible we could simply sell physical copies on physical media and deal with the necessity to build new products every so often?reply

I don't think it was ever the case that games which could theoretically be redistributed we're unprofitable. It's more than that locking everyone into a subscription or renting-as-buying for everything just happens to be more profitable. That's true for just about anything ever in the world, it just so happens that the game, film, and music industries were able to actually pull it off. Other industries suffered from problems of bad public opinion, but the frog is being boiled as we speak, just take a look at the car industry for example. You need to somehow increase the cost of doing the bad thing, and then the natural equilibrium will return to doing the good thing. It's like whenever anyone raises taxes or proposes regulation, someone out there cries about how millionaires or landlords or whoever will all leave. But that rarely happens, if ever, because it's rare that the regulation actually makes something so unprofitable as to not be worth doing, usually it just makes it somewhat less profitable than doing it the unrestricted way.reply
The headline makes it sound like this is specific to NY, but this is a national bill introduced in the House by a NY rep.reply

Even better would be broad copyright reforms. Fair Use needs to be expanded and clarified. History has shown players are able to keep games alive themselves by emulators, reverse engineering, custom servers, etc. Expand Fair Use to say that these things are protected if needed to keep the game functional.reply
How do you define functional?reply
Maintaining the same functionality advertised or realised at the time it was purchased.reply
Consumers always hope that what they gain from a purchase is ownership.reply
This is amazing. So glad to see stuff like this happening.reply

A year ago, I had the opinion that it'd be too expensive for developers to support offline mode, peer to peer, or community servers after shutdown.Today, I don't. I think it's probably a week's worth of work with AI and 1-2 developers.However, enforcing this law is going to be tricky. How well does the peer to peer have to work? How about off line mode? How much support does the developer provide for community servers? Is it only a one-time support?A developer going bankrupt isn't going to be able to do too much.reply

I've long suspected that one of the things that makes monads notoriously difficult to explain to people outside of the Haskell ecosystem is that very few other languages even have a kind system that you are allowed to manipulate in code (and in some, like C++, it's so esoteric that you basically never see it). First explaining that you can even abstract over "type->type" kinded things gets you a lot of the way towards monads without actually describing monads.reply

The problem is not monads. Any programmer understands the need to represent "the world". It is the need to keep that representation modular that leads to monad transformers, which makes regular people (like me) simply check out and go back to C++https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monad_transformerreply

That may be true for functions which operate on a generic Monad typeclass, but typeclasses (Higher kinded types) aren't required to implement concrete Functor / Applicative / Monad instances for a particular type, e.g. Maybe:    fmap f Nothing = Nothing
    fmap f (Just x) = Just (f x)

    pure x = Just x

title: Codex Desktop continuously generates Crashpad pending dumps (github.com/openai)
comments: I'd been running into a lot of disk pressure on my system from agents running. I discovered two main causes:- my approach to using git worktrees for all work. Not entirely surprising, the duplicated build artifacts in each worktree being the main culprit here. There were some limited gains to be had by just being more efficient with how builds were managed but ultimately I just had to limit the number of concurrent features I was working on in a couple of particularly large repos.- more insidious was the fact I was actually hitting memory limits more than I realised and causing my mac to have to swap heavily. The system was surprisingly still quite performant while this was happening... until it wasn't. Unfortunately as best I can tell the only "fix" when this happens is to restart the machine. There's no way to have the system reclaim any of the swap space once it's written to disk. Which if you have it thrash a couple of times a day (especially easy if you leave something running overnight) adds up very quickly.reply
If git used reflink / CoW when available it would make this a lot faster.reply

It's so goddamn bad, I wish it was easier to turn all of this garbage off. I used to spend time defining parallel work lanes to issue to subagents as frontloaded development work with set validation checkpoints and it worked great. Now attempting to do this with 8, 16 subagents will balloon out into hundreds of gigs of fucking messCopy on write worktrees do absolutely nothing to solve this, either. The build artifacts alone will do itreply
switching to copy on write worktrees is the biggest game changer it should become common knowledge pretty soon and it's already available on most operating systemsreply

I ran into similar issues. Sometimes though there are good language specific solutions. For Rust based worktrees you should definitely check out https://mr-boxington.jdx.dev/ .Regarding swapping, are you sure it's not just from ram backed tmpfs partition? For me that was it and most of the swap was from /tmp. So I created an agressive job that runs frequently to delete all tmp files not used in the last ~2 hours without any command holding handles to it.The other thing I found was that there were a bunch of leftover processes from prior coding agents forking commands and just leaving them. So I had to build a system into my agent spawner to automatically launch each agent session in a cgroup whose processes all get killed on task completion.reply

On Linux I’ve taken to disabling swap before doing memory heavy operations. Claude will carelessly run benchmarks and tasks which gobble up all available memory. When that happens, I’m not sure why but my system becomes unresponsive and I can’t kill the process. title: Source code of the Estonian online voting system (github.com/valimised)
comments: Fully software, even a combo of software and hardware, cannot by itself make elections secure.  Think of the Reflections On Trusting Trust problem, the need to verify firmware, etc.  You can't ensure that machines _will_ work correctly, but you _can_ verify that they _did_.  To do verify the machines' functioning after the fact you have to do it very soon after closing of the polls, and you have to devise a manual, statistical random sampling method where you manually check randomly sampled, marked paper ballots, against the digital cast vote record, then do a digital risk limiting audit to check that the CVR totals up to the machines' reported results.  The sooner after closing of the polls you do this, the better the likelihood that any cheating will be caught.  I.e., an immediate manual, partial audit of enough randomly-selected polling locations.That still leaves tons of other technical problems to address, like security of mail-ballots / absentee ballots, the security of ballot boxes used for early voting (because you probably cannot run the above manual partial audit due to then having nightly results available to the public; or maybe you accept that), voter registration, etc.reply

You solve all of these with cryptography.Your ID card contains a private key, you use that key to sign a transaction. It doesn't matter that machine you are running on is compromised as these details can be verified at a later date.Example A:
You vote for candidate A, but software changes to candidate B and software displays that you voted for candidate A. At any later time you can check with an independent device and look at the transaction finding out that it was altered with and retract your vote / change it.Example B:
How do you know your vote was counted? Publish a hash and the signature of every vote, recompute the final tally and compare with all the votes. If your vote is not in the final tally the hash will be different and you can visibly see your vote in the dataset as every transaction is published. To preserve privacy each round has a number, private key + number -> new key so each fingerprint will be unique between votes.reply

> You solve all of these with cryptography.I've spent a lot of time thinking about this problem, and my conclusion is that cryptography alone is not the solution, for reasons like:1. The public needs to believe it, and hypertechnical solutions are a hard sell.2. Any blockchain approach needs to preserve the secrecy of the ballot, otherwise you get all the problems you can expect of non-secret votes (coercion, vote buying, shaming network effects).3. You still need to have the cryptographic rubber meet the physical road _somewehere_ -- it has to, otherwise the need for vote secrecy means that the results can be entirely fictitious and pre-programmed and there is no way to check!I.e., you can have a paperless blockchain solution IFF you abandon vote secrecy.  That is a very tough to swallow pill.On the other hand, if you accept paper ballots and manual partial audits as part of the solution, then blockchain can have a role to play.  For example, the machines could display a blockchain head every 50 ballots cast, and voters take a copy of the blockchain head visible to them, then after the election the public can verify the integrity of the blockchain, and the fact that you only get running tallies every 50 ballots means you get vote secrecy.A system that uses paper ballots and partial manual audits can be explained to the public, and the public can develop confidence in it.  Blockchains can then add a good deal of confidence: the blockchain tells you that the tallies were not modified after the fact, and the partial manual audit tells you to an acceptable level of statistical confidence that the digital cast vote record contains the actual paper ballots _as marked and cast_ by voters.reply

>I.e., you can have a paperless blockchain solution IFF you abandon vote secrecy. That is a very tough to swallow pill.This is false. I know this is a common thought on HN because some formerly popular youtuber did a video about this topic that is still regularly reposted here, but he was already wrong in theory back then and it is certainly wrong in practice today. Secrecy/anonymity and verifiability are no longer mutually exclusive as anyone who is well versed in modern cryptography will be able to tell you.reply
> some formerly popular youtuber did a video about this topicI don't know about this event, do you have a link?reply

I'd appreciate some references.  That's not because I'm trying to put you down with a request for references, but clearly you have seen them, and I'd like to see them.Also, you still have to convince the public.reply

I agree that convincing the public is a separate issue. But on a technical level, these problems are solved. See e.g. this modern implementation: https://github.com/vocdoni/davinci-paper This is a pretty recent one, but the mathematical foundation dates back to the late 80s.There have also been earlier implementations like this one: https://github.com/benadida/helios 
(corresponding paper https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/sec08/tech/full_papers/a...), although it still lacked coercion resistance. But it already uses zero knowledge proofs, which is at the core of anonymous yet verifiable systems.reply

Thanks.  Right, this is zero-knowledge proofs.  I expected as much.  I think that ZK can be made to work for secure voting, though I don't believe that the public can be expected to understand it.  I'll have to read this, but I suspect that there is a way for possessors of secret keys to choose to decrypt ballots and violate ballot secrecy.reply

You know what's easy to understand? Hand marked paper ballots cast anonymously with multiple witnesses to simple optomechanical counting using open hardware and software. The crypto based security can be used to ensure that only a valid ballot enters the vote You have to combine the crypto with a paper trail. Otherwise it can be manipulated by mitm or a bad actor with the keys. Blockchain has more than enough attack vectors.

> Any blockchain approachThis doesn't directly affect your comment, but I'd like to head it off before more occur: "Distributed Database" != "Blockchain".We've had distributed databases with hashes for many decades. It'd be cheap, easy, and fast to run a couple hundred pre-determined nodes controlled by many different governments and institutions who are unlikely to >50% collude.In contrast, the different and new pieces for "Blockchain" all revolve around one root requirement of letting anybody start up an arbitrary number of nodes--which we don't need for elections. Without that requirement, dozens of problems and workarounds fall away, like the problem of voters standing around for transaction clearing times.reply
